guidance: A sizing aid, not a guarantee: journald deletes only archived files, so a journal can sit above its limit until the active file rotates, and compression (on by default) usually stretches the real retention past this estimate. The drop-in names the [Journal] section only; read the current usage with journalctl --disk-usage before and after the change, and keep the KeepFree reserve so the journal cannot crowd out the filesystem.
method: The size limit defaults to 10 % of the filesystem and the KeepFree reserve to 15 %, each capped at 4 GiB; journald honours both and uses the smaller, so the room above the reserve is free space minus the reserve, and the effective limit is the smaller of the size limit and that room. When free space is already inside the reserve the page says so and caps the limit at the free space, because journald raises its limit to what is actually free rather than deleting older entries. The largest journal file defaults to one eighth of the size limit, capped at 128 MiB, and the number of files the limit needs is the size limit divided by that file size, rounded up; above the default SystemMaxFiles=100 the drop-in raises the file count, since 100 files of 128 MiB cannot hold a larger limit. Volatile storage selects the Runtime* settings and measures the /run filesystem instead. Retention is the effective limit divided by the daily volume, printed in hours under one day. Sizes are gibibytes and mebibytes (1024 based), the filesystem size is limited to 0.1 to 100,000 GiB and the daily volume to 0.1 to 100,000 MiB, and the page makes no network request.

journalctl(1) - systemd manual: --disk-usage reports the space the journal files use, the check to run before and after a size change
